comment.body:
Truth is neither absolute nor relative, Julie. 

The problem we've had in our thinking and discussions about "truth" lies in the mistake of pretending that it's a thing that could be of this or that nature. The only non-imaginary, unmanufactured concept of truth I know of is truth as honest relationship to what's actually going on, including the participants interested in knowing what's really going on and their relationships to it and to us. 

Instead, most of us think about truth little differently than a child would. 

A relationship isn't a thing, it's a living, complex phenomenon, a process, a happening, ever changing, moving, folding back on itself, interplaying. 

Truth isn't some "thing" *in relationship* (relative) to other "things". Nor is it a state relative to other states. One of the primary and most important things about truth is that it is not static -- because nothing about which there could be truth, as far as we know, is static in any way that matters.

Truth is honesty about what's going on, our relationship to it, our interaction with it, as well as our relationship to and interaction with others involved in it.

comment.body:
Someone mentioned recently that, more and more, people seem to be just sticking their heads in the sand.

That's understandable, of course. It's what happens when denial becomes untenable but we're still not ready to come clean.

Head in sand is temporary, though: otherwise, they die. Whenever a cult implodes, there's always a gaggle of diehards who go with it.

The rest, one way or the other, pull their heads out.

And we've got to keep in mind where our information is coming from. 99.9% of what's actually happening at any point in time is well beyond our awareness, let alone any reporting.

The truth always comes out. Always. It does its work even though it's rarely admitted and most of its effects are never recognized. It doesn't care. It doesn't need permission or approval.

I'm learning to be more like that. Bottom line, no matter what is or is not going to happen, it doesn't change what I need to do. I still struggle with disillusionment, depression sometimes, but that's all about letting my minuscule 0.1% awareness affect my motivation.

The one thing I have no doubt about is that everything I do will have an effect. The more I do the more effect it will have. Is it enough? Will it be enough? When will it be enough?

Who the hell knows what "enough" is? I certainly don't, and I don't know of a single person who does.

Makes everything really simple.

What should I do? What can I do? What will I do?

Everything I fucking can, along with learning to become even more capable, so that there's less and less "I can't".

❤️

In my version of Sisyphus, he blows the fucking boulder up, flips the gods the bird, and crosses the fucking hill.

Never looks back.

comment.body:
I've maintained a HUGE open window for bloviators to let rip their flatulence, for two reasons:

1. Not every brain fart is 100% toxic. Some actually have some sweet spots that are worth it.

2. Even if a person is utterly chock full of shit, I get to learn how to deal with their ilk and their games.

I spent the majority of my life tolerating these stinky windbags, operating under the delusion that they knew something I didn't.

I finally wised up.

I spent the last 30+ years tolerating them in an extreme version of don't-throw-baby-out-with-bathwater that I've yet to see anyone else even come close to.

I've learned a shit ton.

The last year or two, though, I've found myself getting bored with it. I won't say that I've learned everything I need to know, let alone everything there is to know -- but boredom tells me when I've started to spin wheels letting others spin theirs. 

Besides, if I'm getting bored, I ain't learning shit.

So, my open-for-bullshit window is rapidly closing. I just don't have time or energy or bandwidth to waste on drivel, anymore.

I went well over a decade on social media barely blocking anyone at all. I don't expect that trend to continue.

Just thought I'd FYI y'all.

I've got 10 - 20 years left (barring miracles of actual medical science), and I'm gonna use it as wisely as I can.

It's NOT just "capitalism" -- it's every "system" built on the foundation of "ownership".

 

In other words, it's every socio-economic system ever implemented by what we'd call a "civilized society".

 

Oddly and ironically enough, you'll only find gift and sharing systems among the "uncivilized".

 

Maybe being uncivilized is not at all a bad thing.

 

Ownership is, at essence, the unilaterally declared right of preemptive, causeless deprivation of others. Only the recognition of ownership requires other to agree. The assertion of ownership is undeniably, unequivocally, inevitably, and irremediably (I'd add irredeemably) an act of aggression. So, it's inherently and unavoidably violent, harmful, and injurious.

 

Before you knee-jerk into a defense of ownership, think a moment. What does the evidence show? The vast majority of people thriving in societies built on the principle of deprivation-first-always? Or a minuscule minority riding on the backs of the vast suffering, oppressed majority? Think Sumerians, Babylonians, Greeks, Romans, Medieval Europe, India (caste system), China (burying live servants and soldiers with royals), Egypt, you name it.

 

What does the evidence say about the success (and for whom?) of ownership-based societies?
